newsitem.title: USA: Clinton speech guest highlights racial harmony.
newsitem.headline: Clinton speech guest highlights racial harmony.

text.p: Hillary Rodham Clinton highlighted her husband's call for racial harmony in America through her choice of a seatmate for Tuesday night's State of the Union speech by President Bill Clinton.

At her side was the Rev. Robert Schuller, a television evangelist who had advised the president to use a Bible quote from the prophet Isaiah to stress the need for racial harmony during his Jan. 20 inauguration.

The Clinton family Bible that the president laid his hand on as he took the oath of office Jan. 20 was open to Isaiah 58:12, and in his subsequent inaugural address, he borrowed from the passage to call on Americans to join together as "repairers of the breach."
Mrs. Clinton used the choice of other seatmates to stress some of her top concerns, such as women's issues and improving children's education.
With her was Dr. Kristen Zarfos, a Connecticut physician who has appealed for legislation requiring a longer hospital stay for women after a mastectomy.

In his speech, Clinton appealed to Congress for bipartisan support for legislation requiring hospitals to let women stay in the hospital for 48 hours after a mastectomy. Last year he led a drive to allow new mothers to stay in hospitals 48 hours after birth and end "drive-through deliveries."
Also seated with the first lady was Sue Winski, a Northbrook, Ill., teacher who has been instrumental in improving math and science studies, and two students.

Mrs. Clinton was also seated with Janet Langhart, wife of Defence Secretary William Cohen; Tipper Gore, wife of Vice President Al Gore and a Gore daughter, Sara; Lillie Tejeda, mother of the late Representative Frank Tejeda, D-Texas, who died last week, and his sister, Mary Alice Tejeda-Lara; and three Democratic state governors, Bob Miller of Nevada, Zell Miller of Georgia and Gary Locke of Washington.

The seating arrangements were straight out of the political playbook of former Republican President Ronald Reagan, who started the practice of reinforcing his State of the Union themes by seating people in the visitors' gallery who personified those themes.
